Learning Objectives
Understand the biomechanics of throwing and adaptations to the throwing shoulder.
Define common injury patterns in throwing athletes.
Discuss the appropriate patient history to obtain from and physical examination to perform in
throwing athletes.
Explore nonsurgical and surgical treatment approaches and indications.
Understand rehabilitation principles, prevention, and outcomes.

Throwing athletes have anatomic variations, known as adaptations, that facilitate throwing.
Because of repetitive high stress, the shoulder of throwing athletes is at risk for injury such as:
Labral and superior labrum anterior to posterior (SLAP) tears,
Internal and external impingement
Rotator cuff tears
Identifying deficiencies in throwing mechanics and the kinetic chain is critical to preventing and
managing shoulder problems.
Epidemiology
Approximately 3 million children play youth baseball each year in the United States and 10
million children play youth baseball each year worldwide.1
Approximately 50,000 baseball-related injuries are estimated to occur each year across all
levels. The rate of injury per 100 players per year is as low as 2 in Little League and as high as
58 in the major leagues.2
In the major leagues, shoulder injury rates have declined, with a reciprocal increase in elbow
injuries.3
Approximately 74% of youth baseball players (8 to 18 years) report having had arm pain while
playing baseball (23% with documented injury); 46% of youth baseball players report being
told to play through the pain. The cause of most of these injuries is considered to be overuse.4
Anatomy
Osteology
Scapulothoracic articulation
Articulation between the scapula and thorax (not a true joint); bursa include the infra-
serratus (scapulothoracic) bursa and the supra-serratus (subscapularis) bursa.
The only bony attachment to the thorax is through the clavicle at the acromioclavicular and
sternoclavicular joints.
The scapula spans ribs 2 through 7 and has medial, lateral, and inferior borders.
The suprascapular notch is at the base of the coracoid process. The transverse scapular
ligament spans the notch, with the suprascapular artery typically above the ligament and the
suprascapular nerve below.

The spinoglenoid notch is below the lateral border of the scapular spine, and the
suprascapular artery and nerve traverse it. The spinoglenoid ligament spans the notch.
Biomechanics
Scapular motion
Elevation: trapezius, levator scapulae, rhomboids
Depression: latissimus dorsi
Medial (downward) rotation: latissimus, rhomboids, and levator scapula
Lateral (upward) rotation: lower and middle trapezius, serratus anterior
Protraction: serratus anterior and pectoralis major/minor
Retraction: middle trapezius, latissimus dorsi, and rhomboids
The ratio of glenohumeral-to-scapulothoracic motion during shoulder abduction is 2:1.
As the arm elevates, the center of rotation of the scapula moves superiorly and medially, with
lateral displacement of the inferior angle (lateral rotation).

Biomechanics of Throwing
Pitching motion is broken down into six phases5 (Figure 3)
Wind up
Early cocking
Late cocking
Acceleration
Deceleration
Follow through
Figure 3 Illustration shows the phases of throwing. (Reproduced from Limpisvasti O,

ElAttrache NS, Jobe FW: Understanding shoulder and elbow injuries in baseball. J Am Acad
Orthop Surg 2007;15[3]:139-147.)
Force is transferred from the ground reaction forces through a stable base with mainly lower
extremity movement during wind up.
Maximal stress is placed on the shoulder in late cocking/early acceleration, during which the
shoulder approaches maximal external rotation. The scapula is retracted, the elbow is flexed,
and the humerus is in abduction and external rotation. The subscapularis, pectoralis major,
and latissimus dorsi are eccentrically contracting to stabilize the joint. Most shoulder injuries
occur in this stage.
The acceleration phase is characterized by scapula protraction, humeral adduction, and
internal rotation (force produced by the subscapularis, pectoralis major, and latissimus).
Deceleration results in glenohumeral distraction and shear forces, with eccentric loading of
the posterior rotator cuff and considerable biceps and brachialis activation to slow elbow
extension.
Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Kinetic chain
The term kinetic chain refers to the coordinated, sequential development of force. For
overhead athletes, force is generated in the lower extremities, is transferred through the
trunk, and is delivered by the shoulder (arm position, slot) and the distal upper extremity
(hand speed, whip). Efficient transfer of force is necessary to create velocity.6
Weakness or poor mechanics along the kinetic chain may result in inefficient force generation,
leading to increased stress at the shoulder.6
Adaptations and Subsequent Pathology
Internal Rotation and Total Range of Motion
Glenohumeral internal rotation deficit is defined as an 18° difference in internal rotation
compared with the contralateral extremity.
Total range of motion deficit is defined as more than 5° of asymmetry in total arc of motion.
These are not necessarily causative but may place higher stress on key stabilizing components
of the shoulder6 (Figure 4).

Increased Abduction and External Rotation
Increased humeral retroversion—Increased stress on the humerus during development slows
natural humeral anteversion, resulting in increased retroversion.7
Posterior glenoid dysplasia and retroversion and a hypertrophic posterior labrum may
develop.8
Posterior capsule: chronic tensile load is theorized to thicken the posterior capsule.8
Decreased flexibility results in superior/posterior displacement of the humeral head.
Secondarily, the humeral head impinges the posterior-superior rotator cuff against the
posterior labrum and the glenoid.

Muscular tension is increased after repetitive strain because of increased intramuscular
calcium (secondary to muscle damage); this results in muscle fiber shortening, which peaks
at 4 to 18 hours after a workout.6
Anterior capsule: anterior laxity may develop secondary to tight posterior structures,
referred to as the cam effect.8
Debated by Jobe,9 who claimed internal impingement was accompanied by anterior micro-
instability, and Halbrecht et al,10 who claimed anterior instability should lessen the
symptoms.
Burkhart et al8 described the occurrence of anterior laxity as the cam effect (because of
redundancy of the anterior-inferior capsule).
Peel-Back Mechanism
When the arm is in the 90-90 position, the biceps tendon is shifted more posteriorly (because
of external rotation), and the biceps anchor subsequently twists. This places a torsional force
on the superior labrum.
Although this is a normal adaptation for throwing athletes, it may become pathologic if the
anchor becomes unstable.8
Altered Scapular Motion
SICK scapula11
Scapular malpositioning—The scapula protracts, rotating about a horizontal axis, with the
upper scapula rotating anteroinferiorly; the shoulder appears lower than the contralateral
side.
Inferior medial border prominence
Coracoid pain and malpositioning—Contraction of the pectoralis minor and the short head of
the biceps contribute to the coracoid tilting inferiorly and laterally away from the midline.
Dyskinesis—Decreased subacromial space leads to external impingement and rotator cuff
weakness.
Early in the condition, substantial deficits in range of motion and form (kinetic chain) may be
noted before the onset of symptoms. Failure to address these factors early may lead to
worsening dysfunction and increased risk for intraarticular damage.
Internal impingement (Figure 5)

Deficiencies in the kinetic chain and athletic form
Fatigue of the serratus anterior, which leads to increased rotator cuff and periscapular muscle
activation and increased scapular external rotation13
Deficits in range of motion
Total range-of-motion deficit appears to be most correlated rather than glenohumeral
internal rotation deficit alone (because of limited external rotation).
Increased risk of ulnar collateral ligament injury and medial elbow torque14
Limitation of external rotation leads to decreased arm slot or may allow the arm to lag while
throwing (compensatory to maintain velocity).15

Phase of throwing in which pain occurs
Patients initially describe fatigue and tightness in the shoulder after throwing and an inability
to get loose.
Patients may progress to dead-arm symptoms with loss of control and velocity.
Discomfort typically occurs during the late cocking or early acceleration phase of throwing.
Physical Examination
Evaluate the static shoulder in comparison with the contralateral shoulder; measure the range
of motion with the use of a goniometer (assessing for glenohumeral internal rotation
deficit/total range of motion deficit).
Always assess trunk, core, and lower extremity flexibility; symmetry; balance; and strength.
Scapula—A SICK scapula manifests with the involved shoulder appearing anterior and inferior
(protracted), coracoid tenderness, and dyskinesis.
Scapular retraction test—Manually retract the scapula with the palm/forearm placed on the
scapula and fingers over the coracoid; decreased pain and improved strength with
supraspinatus testing.
Scapular assist—Reduce pain with shoulder elevation by manually assisting the inferior
scapula in abduction/elevation.

Dynamic labral shear test
O’Brien active compression test (Video 1)
Relocation test (pain; Video 2)

Outcomes
Variable and dependent on the specific pathology
In several series, SLAP lesions were successfully managed nonsurgically in approximately
50% of throwing athletes.6,16
Rotator cuff pathology is highly prevalent in throwing athletes and should not be
overmanaged.
Research findings show that 80% of major league throwing athletes with internal
impingement have a rotator cuff tear.6,17
Surgical Management
Indications
Rotator cuff tear
Débridement for partial-thickness tears (<75%) that do not respond to nonsurgical
management18-20
Repair for tears larger than 75% with anterior cable involvement; completion of tear with
restoration of the anterior anchor21 versus transtendinous22 repair.

SLAP tear
Tears with mechanical symptoms not responding to nonsurgical management
Repair of the biceps anchor versus débridement
Need to avoid over-constraining the biceps tendon6
Biceps tenodesis for concomitant biceps tendon pathology
Contraindications
Inadequate trial of nonsurgical management
Outcomes
Highly variable surgical outcomes because of small cohorts, low levels of evidence, and the
high prevalence of concomitant pathology
Rotator cuff repair
Approximately 85% of pitchers who undergo rotator cuff débridement return to sports
activity at their previous level; however, some have experienced continued pain,19,20 and
rates of return to sports activity have been as low as 16% in some series.6
Among pitchers who underwent rotator cuff repairs, 83% returned to sports activity at their
previous level.21
Combined SLAP and rotator cuff repair is associated with poor outcomes in throwing
athletes (57% return to sports activity at their previous level).23
SLAP repair
High variability in return to previous level of play (22% to 94%).6
